newsitem.title: INDIA: Political instability fears rattle Indian bourses.
newsitem.headline: Political instability fears rattle Indian bourses.

text.p: Fears of mounting political instability rattled Indian stocks on Friday for the second day in a row, brokers and analysts said.
At 0941 GMT, the 30-share index of the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) was down 43.90 points, or 1.33 percent, at 3,263.15 after falling 36.87 points on Thursday.
"The market is on the borderline of panic," said BSE broker Ramesh Damani. "The political worries have added to the market's other woes."

The latest nervousness was triggered by fresh criminal charges filed by federal police in a New Delhi court on Thursday against former Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao in connection with a seven-year old forgery case.
Rao was earlier denied anticipatory bail against possible arrest in another criminal conspiracy case in which he was ordered to appear personally in court as a co-accused.
Two other people accused in the case are in jail pending trial.
The ruling minority United Front coalition government of Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda depends on Rao's Congress party's support for its survival.
"The political uncertainty has heightened," said Bharat Iyer, strategist at UBS Securities. "This is the reason for the fall (in share prices) over the last two days."
"The relationship comes under strain," said Iyer.
"The Congress may have to rethink its support to the United Front government," said Vijay Pandya, director at Classic Share and Stock Brokers. "That's why the market is so grim."

"The political risk factor for this government is lower now," said Supra Subramanian, director at Hoare Govett Asia Securities, the investment arm of ABN-AMRO Bank. "This should strengthen the United Front government."

The Congress posed the main threat to the minority coalition because it held the second largest number of seats in the lower house of parliament after the main opposition Bharatiya Janata Party, analysts said.
But with its leader caught in legal troubles and some former ministers facing corruption cases, the party will not want to pull down the government and face another elections, they said.
"Contrary to popular belief it might help the government," said Ketan Jhaveri, head of broking at Kotak Securities. "The Congress might join the government."

Already a faction within the Congress, which has ruled India for all but four years since independence from Britain in 1947, has been wanting to join Deve Gowda's cabinet but the stumbling block was Rao, brokers said.
